newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin, Maskhadov seen signing political deal.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin, Maskhadov seen signing political deal.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin and Chechen leader Aslan Maskhadov will meet on Monday to sign new agreements on political and economic issues.
Interfax news agency quoted Maskhadov as saying that the agreements could "end the war and begin an era of peace" between Russia and Chechnya.

"It removes the ground for the parties of war to trigger confrontation between Moscow and Grozny," he said. Maskhadov said his top-level delegation of ministers and advisers had arrived "with peace and in the name of peace".
Russia's Itar-Tass news agency quoted "informed sources" as saying that the two men were due to sign a political agreement and agreements on economic and social issues.
Monday's talks, due to start at noon (0800 GMT), will be the first meeting between the two men since before Maskhadov was elected Chechen president in January.
He has vowed to fight for full independence for his Transcaucasus region, a demand which Moscow rejects out of hand.
Tens of thousands of people died in an ill-fated Russian military operation to crush Chechnya's independence drive.
A peace deal sealed last year included the withdrawal of Russian troops and a Chechen promise not to raise the painful issue of its future status until 2001.
There has been no indication that the two sides have reached a final agreement on the status of the region.
"The negotiation commissions have exhausted their resources and it is now for the presidents to decide," Tass quoted chief Russian negotiator Ivan Rybkin as saying.

The meeting takes place two days after gunmen kidnapped a Russian television crew in Chechnya, posing a new challenge for the separatist leaders and souring the atmosphere before the talks with Yeltsin.
It was the latest in a series of kidnappings and Russian officials said these, together with two explosions in southern Russia, had complicated the prospects for talks.
Both sides have thrown responsibility for the events on unspecified "parties of war" which want to wreck the peace process.
